stories.title: ESA's Hera spacecraft returns first close-up of the Didymos asteroid system after DART
paragraphs: The European Space Agency says its Hera planetary-defence spacecraft has acquired its first close-up of the Didymos binary asteroid system. ESA released the image on Nov. 5, 2026; Space.com covered it as the Nov. 6 Space photo of the day.

According to ESA, the monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera took the image from about 60 kilometers away. The agency describes Didymos as about 780 meters across; Dimorphos, about 151 meters across, is mostly hidden in shadow in this frame. Space.com similarly describes Didymos as about 780 meters wide and Dimorphos as roughly 160 meters across, with only a sliver of the moonlet visible.

ESA and Space.com both quote Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel saying the first reaction was "wow," and that the view shows the opposite side of Didymos from the face NASA's DART camera imaged before impact. Michel notes the equatorial ridge remains, but that this side also shows multiple boulders, craters, and patterns that look like grooves or ridges.

ESA says NASA's roughly 580-kilogram DART craft struck Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, at about 6.1 kilometers per second and shortened Dimorphos's orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes. Mission scientist Michael Kueppers said ejected material may have crossed the roughly 1-kilometer gap to Didymos and could explain some of the new surface features. ESA says detailed images of both asteroids are planned for unveiling on Nov. 25, 2026.

image.alt: ESA Hera image of asteroid Didymos with a sliver of Dimorphos visible

stories.title: Scientists find chemically confirmed dinosaur blood molecules in 115-million-year-old bones
paragraphs: ScienceDaily reports that a Curtin University–led team found fossilized red blood cells and chemical evidence of blood molecules inside 115-million-year-old bones of Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating theropod from northeastern Brazil. The findings appear in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

According to the ScienceDaily release of Curtin University materials, researchers identified mineralized red blood cells in vascular canals and detected preserved heme molecules—components of hemoglobin—calling it the first definitive chemical confirmation of hemoglobin-derived molecules inside fossilized dinosaur red blood cells. The work also reports amino acids associated with collagen.

Curtin's Kliti Grice, quoted in the release, said detecting intact heme-derived molecules in cells that old is a landmark result. The release links the preservation to the mineral hausmannite and to rapid burial in a low-oxygen setting with abundant microbial activity.

The international team included researchers from Curtin University, Japan's Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, Brazil's National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri, and Johns Hopkins University. The release says the work challenges assumptions that hemoglobin-related molecules cannot survive deep time and may inform searches for ancient life beyond Earth.

image.alt: Illustration related to dinosaur blood preserved in fossil bone

stories.title: JWST 'digital twin' unmasks exoplanet 51 Eridani b below the telescope's stability limit
paragraphs: Live Science reports that Northwestern University astronomers used a physics-based method called FLIP (Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets) on James Webb Space Telescope data to reveal giant exoplanet 51 Eridani b, previously drowned out by stellar glare in JWST observations. The results were published Nov. 4, 2026, in Nature.

According to Live Science and Universe Today, FLIP builds a "digital twin" of how light travels through JWST, accounting for tiny shifts and vibrations that standard reference-star subtraction misses. First author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez said planets can be a million times fainter than their stars, so glare removal is essential. Co-author Jason Wang stressed the approach uses physics-informed modeling with machine-learning techniques and is not an AI model that invents the planet.

Universe Today notes the team tested FLIP on 51 Eridani, about 97 light-years away, at the 4.3 μm wavelength used for carbon dioxide studies. The Nature paper, as summarized there, reports sensitivity 2–15 times better than standard techniques and the first detection of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 μm—more than 5 sigma in the processed JWST/NIRCam F430M data.

Both outlets say the method could help future observatories such as the Habitable Worlds Observatory image fainter planets by easing ultrastability requirements. Ferrer-Chavez said solar-system-like planets likely exist but remain hard to see until techniques improve.

image.alt: JWST views of 51 Eridani before and after FLIP starlight removal

stories.title: China's Tiangong space station sets a record-low temperature with ultracold atoms
paragraphs: Science News reports that researchers cooled about 20,000 rubidium atoms aboard China's Tiangong space station to roughly 10 picokelvins—about 10 trillionths of a kelvin above absolute zero (−273.15°C)—forming a Bose-Einstein condensate colder than any previously reported. The results appear in Science on Nov. 5, 2026.

According to Science News, the team used laser-based traps to slow the atoms' motion. Temperature in these systems is defined by how slowly the atom cloud spreads when released. Microgravity on the station avoids the sagging that gravity causes in Earth-bound cold-atom clouds.

Science News says earlier spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates on the International Space Station reached effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins, and an Earth drop-tower experiment reached 38 picokelvins. Drop-tower free fall is brief; orbital microgravity is not, which is why space experiments can push colder.

The magazine notes that ultracold atoms let researchers study exotic quantum states of matter and test ideas such as the equivalence principle—the notion that objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

stories.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with 15-second video clips
paragraphs: On Nov. 5, 2026, Google said Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud. Product manager Anish Nangia wrote that the update adds native video up to 15 seconds (up from 10 seconds on Omni 1.1), multi-turn conversational editing, stronger reference following, and a 30% price cut to $0.07 per second for 720p video.

According to the Google DeepMind post, creators can draft at 360p or 720p, fix details with follow-up edits instead of regenerating whole clips, then upscale selected results to 1080p or 4K. Duration can be set in one-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds.

Google says the model holds character, product, and style references—including faces, garments, packaging type, and brand colors—more consistently across camera moves, and supports short motion clips up to three seconds plus audio cues. Multi-turn edits can swap backgrounds, lighting, weather, or aspect ratio without restarting from scratch.

The company also cites more natural multi-speaker dialogue and lip-sync, steadier cinematic camera moves with fewer jump cuts, and an imperceptible SynthID watermark on outputs. Provisioned Throughput is available for enterprise use on Google Cloud.

stories.title: OpenAI launches Images 2.6 with GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst
paragraphs: On Nov. 4, 2026, OpenAI's community announcement said ChatGPT Images 2.6 plus GPT-Image-2.6 Flare and Sunburst are coming to the API with 50% faster image generation, GIF creation, reusable reference images, image markup, and SVG exports.

According to that announcement and MarkTechPost's launch coverage, Flare is the faster API model—generating images in as little as six seconds—while Sunburst targets higher-quality generation and stronger consistency across edits.

MarkTechPost, summarizing OpenAI's Images 2.6 launch materials, reports that Images 2.6 is available in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API; that a new complexity parameter offers low, medium, and high planning levels (default high); and that OpenAI says people now create more than 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT and the API.

MarkTechPost lists token pricing for Flare and Sunburst as identical on OpenAI's model pages and notes GIF and SVG output through the Image API. The community post links readers to the full release announcement, model cards, and pricing.
